description: A nurse looking to work with others across various fields to create this project of Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
summary: Our project is an autonomous, nurse-led clinical decision support app that helps astronauts detect and manage Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) and microgravity fluid and electrolyte shifts during deep-space missions with communication delays. By passively syncing wearable sensors (smart contact lenses, cranial fluid headbands, mobile LBNP gravity pants) with ISS diagnostic tools (OCT, handheld ocular ultrasound, tonometer, i-STAT blood analyzer), the app tracks eye and head pressure alongside sodium, potassium, osmolality, and hematocrit levels without manual data entry. Designed to eliminate hospital alarm fatigue, it uses a calming light-green interface, simple plus or minus baseline indicators, and a gently vibrating color-coded wristband to alert crew members to physiological drifts. When yellow or red thresholds trigger, plain-English action cards guide astronauts through safe bedside interventions, such as -25 mmHg LBNP sessions, hydration balancing, and video-guided checks, while flagging Acetazolamide (Diamox) escalation for Crew Medical Officer or Flight Surgeon review with automatic potassium and hydration safety checks.
details:
Project Research & Design: Autonomous SANS & Electrolyte Management App

Our project for the NASA Space Apps Challenge is designed to help astronauts actively manage and mitigate Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) and fluid shifts during long-duration missions. Because microgravity naturally pulls bodily fluids upward toward the head and chest, astronauts face serious physiological risks that require constant attention. 

In microgravity, the body's hormone systems like the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) shift, causing the kidneys to excrete less sodium. Combined with prepackaged space food, which is usually packed with salt, this can elevate Sodium levels, making the astronauts hold on to water even more. Coupled with the tendency for cephalad fluid shift in microgravity, where fluid pools in the head and chest, it increases the risk for SANS/exacerbates SANS. Our application empowers crew members to detect early changes in their health and apply timely, independent interventions. By giving astronauts clear, actionable insights, the app reduces cognitive overload and minimizes the need to contact flight surgeons and other healthcare providers on Earth for routine bedside guidance, which is especially critical as deep-space missions experience longer communication delays.

To give a complete picture of an astronaut's condition, the platform organizes health tracking into two primary data categories alongside a quick symptom check. The first category focuses on eye and head fluid metrics. It displays intraocular pressure as a straightforward reading in millimeters of mercury, monitors optic nerve swelling using handheld eye ultrasound and Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) scans to see if fluid is pressing against the back of the eye, and tracks directional trends in head fluid pooling. We also have a section to track Visual Acuity. We have Video Demonstrations under each intervention on the app. The second category monitors blood and electrolytes, specifically sodium and potassium, which regulate fluid retention, muscle function, and heart rhythm in space. By pairing these levels with hydration and blood concentration markers like osmolality and hematocrit, the app helps distinguish true dehydration from simple fluid redistribution. Finally, if sensors detect a sudden physiological drift away from baseline, the app triggers a fast, ten-second tap prompt asking the astronaut if they are experiencing blurry near vision, head fullness, headaches, or dizziness. 

Because astronauts operate on demanding schedules, we designed the data collection workflow to run with as little friction as possible. Rather than interrupting a crew member's workday, the system relies heavily on passive background streaming combined with quick periodic uploads. Background auto-syncing integrates seamlessly with wearable hardware, such as a smart contact lens for continuous eye pressure, as well as a fluid-sensing headband for cranial tissue fluid shifts, and mobile Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) gravity pants, which are in development at NASA currently. Pressure numbers and suit suction levels stream automatically to the app via Bluetooth Low Energy and local cabin Wi-Fi without manual entry. Every few days, or when prompted by the app, astronauts can also take readings using the ISS handheld ocular ultrasound, OCT scanner, or the i-STAT finger-prick blood analyzer, with all results auto-populating directly into the dashboard with zero manual typing.

When an astronaut opens the app, they are greeted by a calm interface designed for a two-second glance rather than a cluttered hospital monitor full of tiny numbers and loud alarms. We went with the color light green because that is one of the colors that astronauts prefer, as it lightens their mood and reduces visual fatigue. On the screen, values glow green when levels are steady, warm yellow when a mild drift is detected, and red when action is needed. These colors light up around the card decks. Different cards display different short and clear information so anyone, even without medical training, can immediately see if fluid is building up behind the eyes. One card shows the latest sodium and potassium readings with + and – signs to show when the level goes up or below baseline, removing the need for astronauts to memorize normal lab ranges while still allowing them to tap either electrolyte reading for detailed historical graphs. When everything is normal, the bottom of the screen stays completely blank with a dark green outline around the values and text. However, if a drift occurs, a color-matched action card slides up from the bottom with plain-English instructions, such as turning on the gravity pants to -25mmHg for twenty minutes and drinking water. Once the crew member completes the step and taps done, the card slides back down and logs the intervention.

To ensure astronauts never miss an important update while working around the station, the app pairs with a lightweight companion wristband that replaces jarring alarms with calm, non-intrusive buzzing alerts. Whenever the app's top status ring shifts to a yellow or red color, the wristband lights up in the matching color and delivers a gentle vibration on the wrist. It also shows the alerted values on the wristband, so that they can conveniently peek at it without opening the full app. This quiet sync allows crew members to stay aware of subtle bodily changes wherever they are on the spacecraft without adding stress or noise to their environment.

Ultimately, our solution stands apart by combining realistic spaceflight protocols with a focused, human-centered design. While NASA is actively developing a broad, Earth-independent Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) to assist crews with general medical decisions, our app zooms in specifically on SANS and electrolyte shifts, translating complex data into the kind of calm bedside care astronauts would normally receive from nurses and physicians on Earth. Every prompt is grounded in NASA's real Medical Operations and Clinical Care guidelines and draws directly from the medications and oral or IV supplies listed on the actual ISS Medical Kit Checklist. Furthermore, the platform bridges the gap between current and future space medicine. It works right away with active ISS equipment like the i-STAT, tonometer, OCT, and ocular ultrasound, while remaining ready to integrate next-generation wearables tracked on NASA TechPort, such as cranial fluid headbands, mobile LBNP suits, and non-invasive sweat electrolyte sensors that will eventually eliminate finger-prick fatigue altogether.

Studies note that around -25mmHg is a sweet spot to move some blood away from the head and chest to other parts of the body. Anything stronger can pull too much blood from the brain, making astronauts lightheaded and dizzy. Using the LBNP machine for 20-30 mins allows for a safe enough speed of circulating fluid all over the body.

Pharmacologic Escalation Safety Check:

Acetazolamide (Diamox) is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor already carried in the ISS Oral Medication Pack. Works in the eye to lower aqueous humor production (reducing IOP) and in the brain's choroid plexus to slow cerebrospinal fluid production (reducing ICP and relieving optic nerve swelling). In our app, if non-drug countermeasures fail to bring red-zone eye/head pressure down, the app flags the reading for Flight Surgeon / Crew Medical Officer (CMO) review before Acetazolamide is taken (especially since Acetazolamide acts as a diuretic and can lower potassium levels. This would then require close electrolyte tracking on the dashboard).
